meta.title: Intangible assets and goodwill
meta.summary: Characteristics and recognition of intangible assets, amortization of limited-life intangibles, types of intangibles, research and development costs, goodwill in a business combination, and impairment of intangibles and goodwill.

videos.title: What intangible assets are
videos.take: Purchased intangibles are capitalized; internally created ones are mostly expensed; limited lives are amortized

scenes.say: Welcome to Intermediate Accounting Two. Bluestem Outdoor is growing up: new brands, new debt, and soon, public shareholders. We start with assets you can't touch.
Intangible assets lack physical substance and aren't financial instruments. Patents, trademarks, customer lists, licenses and goodwill are examples. Their value comes from rights and advantages.

scenes.heading: How they're recorded
scenes.say: Purchased intangibles are recorded at cost, including legal fees and other costs to acquire them. Internally created ones are mostly expensed as incurred: only direct costs like legal and registration fees are capitalized.

scenes.heading: Amortization
scenes.say: Intangibles with a limited life are amortized over their useful life, usually straight-line, and tested for impairment when events suggest it. Those with an indefinite life, like a renewable trademark, aren't amortized but are tested at least annually.
Use the shorter of legal life and economic life. A patent may last twenty years legally but be obsolete in six.
Quick check. Which intangible is not amortized? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, the indefinitely renewable trademark. It's tested for impairment instead.

videos.title: Types of intangibles: the patent
videos.take: Six categories of intangibles; a patent's cost and successful defense costs are amortized over its useful life

scenes.say: Bluestem buys a patent on a folding-kayak hinge from an inventor in Duluth.

scenes.heading: Six types
scenes.say: Intangibles fall into six groups: marketing-related, like trademarks; customer-related, like customer lists; artistic-related, like copyrights; contract-related, like franchises and licenses; technology-related, like patents; and goodwill.

scenes.heading: The hinge patent
scenes.say: Bluestem pays $180,000 including legal fees. The patent has fifteen years of legal life left, but Bluestem expects the design to stay useful for six. Amortization is $30,000 a year.

scenes.heading: Year-end amortization
scenes.say: Amortization is often credited directly to the asset account, though an accumulated amortization account is also used.

If Bluestem successfully defends the patent in court, the $24,000 of legal costs are added to the patent and amortized over its remaining life. If it loses, the costs are expensed and the patent written off.

scenes.q: Patent cost $90,000; legal life 12 years; useful life 5 years. Annual amortization?
scenes.say: Quick check. Patent cost ninety thousand; legal life twelve years; useful life five. Annual amortization? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Research and development costs
videos.take: US GAAP expenses R&D as incurred; IFRS capitalizes development costs that meet criteria

scenes.say: Bluestem spends $350,000 designing an electric-assist kayak. Is that an asset?
Under US GAAP, research and development costs are expensed as incurred, because their future benefits are too uncertain. That includes the salaries, materials, prototypes and testing.

scenes.heading: Bluestem's e-kayak project
scenes.say: Engineers' salaries of $210,000, prototypes of $80,000, outside consultants of $45,000, and depreciation of $15,000 on a test tank are all R&D expense: $350,000.
Notice the test tank. Because it has alternative future uses, Bluestem capitalized it and charges only the year's depreciation to R&D. Equipment built for one project only is expensed immediately.

scenes.heading: GAAP vs IFRS
scenes.say: IFRS expenses research but capitalizes development costs once technical feasibility and other criteria are met. US GAAP has similar rules only for software. Not R&D at all: routine product improvements and quality control.

scenes.q: Under US GAAP, prototype testing costs for a new kayak are:
scenes.say: Quick check. Under US GAAP, prototype testing costs for a new kayak are what? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Goodwill
videos.take: Goodwill = purchase price − fair value of identifiable net assets; it's recorded only in a business combination

scenes.say: Bluestem buys Northwind Canoe Company, a respected canoe maker, for $2.4 million cash.

scenes.heading: Fair values of Northwind's net assets
scenes.say: Bluestem identifies and values every asset it acquires at fair value, including the Northwind trademark and customer list that weren't on Northwind's books. Identifiable assets total $2.6 million, less $700,000 of liabilities: $1.9 million. It paid $2.4 million, so goodwill is $500,000.

sub: The excess paid over fair value
scenes.say: Goodwill is the excess of the purchase price over the fair value of identifiable net assets: reputation, workforce, synergies. It's recorded only when a business is acquired. Internally generated goodwill is never recorded.
Public companies don't amortize goodwill; they test it for impairment. Private companies like Bluestem today can elect to amortize it over ten years or less.

sub: Price < fair value of net assets:
scenes.say: If the price were less than the fair value of net assets, after rechecking the values, Bluestem would record a gain on bargain purchase.

scenes.q: Price $5 million; fair value of identifiable assets $6 million; liabilities $2 million. Goodwill?
scenes.say: Quick check. Price five million; fair value of identifiable assets six million; liabilities two million. Goodwill? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Impairment of intangibles and goodwill
videos.take: Limited-life intangibles use the recoverability test; indefinite-life and goodwill compare carrying amount with fair value

scenes.say: Two years after the purchase, canoe sales slump. Are the Northwind intangibles impaired?

scenes.heading: Three impairment models
scenes.say: Limited-life intangibles use the same two-step test as PP&E. Indefinite-life intangibles skip recoverability: if carrying amount exceeds fair value, the excess is the loss. Goodwill is tested at the reporting unit level.

scenes.heading: Northwind reporting unit
scenes.say: The Northwind reporting unit's carrying amount, including $500,000 of goodwill, is $2.35 million. Its fair value is $2.1 million. The $250,000 excess is the goodwill impairment loss, limited to the goodwill balance.

scenes.heading: Recording
scenes.say: Bluestem records a $250,000 loss in continuing operations. Goodwill impairments can never be reversed.

sub: If impairment isn't more likely than not,
scenes.say: Companies may first do a qualitative assessment: if it's not more likely than not that the unit's fair value is below carrying amount, no further test is needed that year.

scenes.q: Reporting unit carrying amount $8m including goodwill $1m; fair value $6.5m. Goodwill impairment?
scenes.say: Quick check. Reporting unit carrying amount eight million, including one million of goodwill; fair value six point five million. Goodwill impairment? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, $1 million: limited to the goodwill balance.

videos.title: Other costs and presentation
videos.take: Start-up, organization, advertising and initial operating losses are expensed; intangibles are shown separately

scenes.say: Bluestem opens a new store in Minneapolis. Can the opening costs be an asset?

scenes.heading: Always expensed
scenes.say: No. Start-up and pre-opening costs, organization costs, advertising and initial operating losses are expensed as incurred, however much future benefit management expects.

scenes.heading: Minneapolis store opening
scenes.say: Training of $18,000 and $25,000 of opening advertising are expenses. Only the $140,000 of store fixtures, which are property, plant and equipment, are capitalized.

scenes.heading: Presentation
scenes.say: On the balance sheet, goodwill appears on its own line, and other intangibles net of amortization. Amortization and impairment losses go in continuing operations. Notes show classes, useful lives and the next five years' expected amortization.
The irony: Bluestem's own brand, perhaps its most valuable asset, isn't on its balance sheet. Northwind's brand is, because Bluestem bought it.
Quick check. Which of these is capitalized? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, the purchased customer list.

warmup: Name three of Bluestem's most valuable assets that don't appear on its balance sheet. Why aren't they there?
Brand, workforce, designs, dealer relationships: internally generated intangibles are expensed.
acts: Classify each intangible by type: trademark 'Bluestem'; dealer list bought from a competitor; kayak design patent; license to use a hull shape; photo library.
Bluestem buys a patent for $240,000 (legal life 12 years, useful life 8) on January 1; successfully defends it for $36,000 at the start of year 3. Compute amortization in years 1 and 3.
Classify as R&D or not: prototype testing; quality control on production line; lab equipment with alternative uses (cost $60,000, 5 years); seasonal design changes; market research.
R&D; not; capitalize, $12,000 depreciation is R&D; not R&D; not R&D (expense).
Bluestem pays $3,200,000 for a company with identifiable assets at fair value $3,500,000 and liabilities $800,000. Compute goodwill. What if the price were $2,500,000?
Indefinite-life trademark: carrying $300,000, fair value $260,000. Goodwill unit: carrying $4m (incl. goodwill $600,000), fair value $4.2m. Impairment?
Classify: pre-opening rent of new store; legal fees to incorporate; TV ads; store fixtures; employee training.
case: Bluestem paid $2,400,000 for Northwind. Its book net assets were $1,200,000, but fair values include: trademark $300,000 (indefinite life), customer list $150,000 (5 years), patents $90,000 (3 years) and other net assets $1,360,000. The founder wants to put the entire $1.2 million excess into goodwill 'to avoid amortization'.
Compute identifiable net assets and goodwill.
What's wrong with the founder's suggestion?
How does Bluestem's private status affect goodwill?

Identifiable net assets 1,900,000; goodwill 500,000. Identifiable intangibles must be recognized separately at fair value; pushing them into goodwill misstates assets and income. Amortization: customer list 30,000 + patents 30,000 = 60,000; trademark not amortized. Private company alternative: may amortize goodwill (≤10 years) and simplify impairment testing; lost once public.
exam: Explain the accounting for R&D under US GAAP and IFRS, and why GAAP expenses most R&D.
GAAP expenses R&D (uncertain benefits; equipment with alternative uses capitalized). IFRS capitalizes development when criteria met. Comparability and reliability trade-offs.
Compute goodwill and record a later impairment: price $2.4m; identifiable net assets $1.9m; two years later unit carrying $2.35m, fair value $2.1m.
Goodwill 500,000; impairment 250,000; Dr Loss / Cr Goodwill.
